Former athletes and coaches banter on a more-or-less equal footing with other guys who've never played a down or never hiked a ball but have a head full of stats and an encyclopedic knowledge of the manly arts. Watch the 'Ladies in the Locker Room' » . The show is the brainchild of Hattie Lemon, a prolific writer, director, producer and actor whose independent crime series "Atlanta Homicide" is featured on the CoLours TV network. "Ladies in the locker room are not women who think they know everything about sports; they just know the men who do," Lemon said. It's one of the catchphrases she uses to describe the show that immediately disarms most critics who otherwise wouldn't respect an all-female sports show. "It's all women, all sports, all sexy," Lemon said. "It's a combination of my love of sports and my love of media." Each year for the past five years, Lemon has recruited a new group of personalities and production crew members to punch out about a half-dozen shows. The show is captured live at sports clubs and restaurants across the Atlanta metro area, with additional time in the studio to create produced segments to add to the mix.  Photo gallery: Making 'Ladies in the Locker Room' » . And for the second time in the show's history, Lemon is traveling to the Super Bowl with a handful of her ladies and a production crew to create a version of the show featuring interviews with the celebrities and stars flocking to football's big game. Soma Balber, a self-professed superfan of the Los Angeles Lakers basketball team and one of the show's commentators for the 2008-09 season, first got to know Lemon when she began playing a recurring role in "Atlanta Homicide." They got to talking about sports, and Balber was asked to be a part of the show. "It's kind of nice to show the audience that women can have fun watching sports," Balber said. "And we want to educate women about sports as well." Lemon, who describes herself as a huge fan of professional football, says she hopes her show will lead more men to understand that women love sports, too. "When women talk about sports, sometimes men look at us as groupies," Lemon said. "Men don't think women understand sports." As for men who have never played sports but still know all the stats? They get the "man pass." It's not fair, she says, but "it is what it is. I just hope we get more women talking about sports."

**Hattie Lemon’s all-female sports show blends analysis, personality and a distinctly Atlanta perspective in a space long dominated by men.**

**ATLANTA** — In a city where sports loyalties run deep, Hattie Lemon is working to broaden the lineup of voices discussing the games, athletes and moments that keep fans talking.

Her Atlanta-based show, **“Ladies in the Locker Room,”** features an all-female team tackling sports with the same mix of insight, debate and personality traditionally associated with mainstream studio programs. The difference is clear from the title: Women are not appearing as occasional guests or side commentators. They are leading the conversation.

That distinction matters in a sports-media landscape where women have often had to overcome assumptions about their knowledge, fandom and authority. “Ladies in the Locker Room” challenges those conventions simply by putting women in every chair and allowing them to cover sports without treating their presence as a novelty.

The region is home to passionate professional and college fan bases, with football, basketball, baseball and other sports forming part of the city’s cultural rhythm. Programs such as Lemon’s can be local in identity while participating in a national conversation about who gets to talk about sports — and who is viewed as an expert.

Its all-female format does not mean the show speaks with one voice. Part of the appeal of sports debate is disagreement: different teams, different predictions and different interpretations of the same play. By creating room for women to bring their own experiences and opinions, “Ladies in the Locker Room” avoids presenting female fandom as a single point of view.

The show’s name carries its own message. The locker room has long symbolized access — a place where athletes, reporters and insiders shape the stories fans later hear. By placing “ladies” in that space, Lemon’s program reclaims the imagery and makes an argument about belonging.

**Hattie Lemon Builds a Sports Talk Show Where Women Lead the Conversation**

Hattie Lemon saw a gap in sports media: Women were watching games, analyzing teams and debating trades, but they were rarely treated as the central voices in the conversation.

Her response was to create a sports talk show where women could discuss the latest headlines, explain the intricacies of different games and confront outdated assumptions about female fans. The program combines analysis and education with the kind of lively debate familiar to sports audiences—while placing women’s perspectives at the center.

Lemon designed the show for both dedicated followers and viewers who want to understand sports better. Discussions can move from strategy and statistics to athletes, league policies and broader cultural issues. By breaking down terminology and providing context, the hosts aim to make sports more accessible without diluting the analysis.

That educational approach is central to Lemon’s vision. The show does not assume that every viewer already knows the rules or follows every roster move. Instead, it creates space for questions and treats learning as part of being a fan.

At the same time, Lemon wants the program to challenge a persistent stereotype: that women who talk about sports are less informed, less serious or interested only because of a player’s appearance or a family connection. On her show, women are not guests brought in to offer a “female point of view.” They are the analysts, interviewers and authorities driving the discussion.

The format also allows women to be fans in different ways. Some may focus on data and tactics; others may be drawn to history, culture or the personal stories behind competition. Lemon’s larger point is that there is no single test for being an authentic sports fan.

Creating the show has therefore been about more than representation on screen. It is an effort to broaden who is considered credible in sports media and who feels invited into the audience. The program gives experienced fans a place to see their knowledge reflected while helping newcomers build confidence.

Lemon’s show enters a media landscape in which women remain underrepresented in many prominent sports-commentary roles, despite making up a significant part of the fan base. By combining informed conversation with an open, welcoming tone, she is working to change both the image of the sports expert and the image of the sports fan.

For Lemon, the premise is straightforward: Women have always had opinions about sports. Her show makes sure they have the platform to express them—and the authority to be heard.

# Women crash sports TV’s ‘guys’ club’

**By CNN Entertainment**  
**NEW YORK (CNN) —** On most sports-talk programs, the formula is familiar: a desk, a stack of statistics and several men arguing over who should start at quarterback.

“The Clubhouse,” a new weekly television roundtable, is betting viewers are ready for a different lineup.

The program features four women — a veteran sportswriter, a former professional athlete, a broadcaster and a self-described “walking sports encyclopedia” — offering commentary, analysis and trivia on everything from the NFL playoff picture to baseball’s hot-stove season.

There is no token female voice seated between male hosts. Here, the women run the conversation.

“We’re not trying to prove women can talk sports,” host Dana Mercer said during a recent taping. “Women have always talked sports. We’re just putting that conversation on television.”

## More than sideline questions

For years, women on sports broadcasts were most visible as sideline reporters, studio anchors or interviewers. “The Clubhouse” places them in roles traditionally reserved for male commentators: debating strategy, challenging coaching decisions and predicting which teams will survive the postseason.

A recent episode moved quickly from a discussion of an NBA coach’s late-game substitutions to a rapid-fire trivia round about World Series history. The panelists disagreed loudly, interrupted one another and laughed when a supposedly easy hockey question stumped the entire table.

In other words, it looked a lot like sports television.

The difference, producers say, is not that the panel avoids the familiar arguments. It is that the show approaches them without reproducing the locker-room atmosphere that has defined much of the genre.

“We wanted energy, but not four people shouting the same opinion at once,” executive producer Marla Reyes said. “The audience should come away entertained, but also knowing something it didn’t know before.”

## A changing audience

The program arrives as leagues and television networks increasingly recognize women as a substantial part of the sports audience. Women buy tickets, manage fantasy teams, follow recruiting news and spend hours on sports blogs and message boards.

Yet prime-time sports commentary remains overwhelmingly male.

Former soccer player and panelist Keisha Grant said that imbalance can create the false impression that female fans are interested only in personalities or off-field stories.

“If I question a defensive scheme, somebody will still ask who taught me football,” Grant said. “Nobody asks a male commentator whether his father explained the zone blitz to him.”

The show does not ignore fashion, celebrity relationships or the business of sports, but its creators bristle at suggestions that those subjects are included simply because the hosts are women.

“Male shows talk about contracts, scandals and what athletes are wearing all the time,” Mercer said. “Somehow, when we do it, it becomes ‘women’s content.’”

## Winning over skeptics

Not everyone is convinced. Before the first episode aired, online commenters questioned whether the panel had enough credibility — criticism the hosts expected.

Sports media analyst Robert Klein said the program’s biggest challenge may be escaping the novelty label.

“If it is marketed only as ‘the women’s sports show,’ it risks being treated as a side project,” Klein said. “Its long-term success will depend on whether viewers see the panelists as authorities, not symbols.”

The hosts say they welcome scrutiny, as long as they are judged by the same standards as their male counterparts.

“If I make a bad prediction, call me on it,” statistician and trivia specialist Lauren Cho said. “Just remember that guys on television pick the wrong Super Bowl winner every year and still come back Monday morning.”

That line drew the loudest laugh of the taping.

For now, “The Clubhouse” is relying on a mix of sharp opinions, friendly competition and the chemistry among its panelists. Producers are also inviting viewers to submit trivia questions by e-mail and, in a nod to the changing media landscape, to continue debates on the show’s blog and Twitter feed.

The set may look different from the traditional sports-talk desk, but Mercer said the goal is simple.

“We want fans to argue with us,” she said. “That’s the point of sports talk. We just want everyone to get used to the fact that the experts don’t always look like the guys’ club.”
